front: What words create a fee simple determinable, and what does the grantor keep?
back: Durational words (so long as, while, until). The grantor keeps a possibility of reverter; title returns automatically when the event occurs.

front: What creates a fee simple subject to condition subsequent, and how does it end?
back: Conditional words (but if, provided that) plus a reserved right of entry. It ends only when the grantor elects to terminate within a reasonable time; delay may waive.

front: What is a fee simple subject to executory limitation?
back: A fee that ends automatically on a stated event and passes to a third party, who holds a shifting executory interest subject to the RAP.

front: If a third party's executory interest after a defeasible fee violates the RAP, what is left?
back: Strike the gift over. Durational words leave a fee simple determinable with a possibility of reverter in the grantor; conditional words leave the grantee a fee simple absolute.

front: How do courts treat words of purpose such as 'for school purposes'?
back: As a statement of motive, creating a fee simple absolute; courts avoid forfeiture and prefer condition subsequent (or a covenant) over a determinable fee.

front: How does California treat a fee simple determinable?
back: Abolished: it is a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent, and the grantor holds a power of termination that expires 30 years after recording unless a notice of intent to preserve is recorded (Civ. Code §§ 885.020, 885.030).

front: Who may transfer a life estate, and how long does the transferee hold?
back: The life tenant may transfer, but the transferee holds only for the measuring life; a lease by the life tenant ends at the life tenant's death.

front: What are a life tenant's financial duties to the remainderman?
back: Pay property taxes and mortgage interest (not principal) and make ordinary repairs, up to the income or rental value of the land; no duty to insure the remainder.

front: Define affirmative, permissive and ameliorative waste.
back: Affirmative: harmful acts such as exploiting resources. Permissive: failure to repair or pay taxes and interest. Ameliorative: value-increasing change in character, allowed if remaindermen would not reasonably object or conditions have changed.

front: What is the open-mines doctrine?
back: A life tenant may continue mining operations already open when the life estate began, and may take resources for repairs and reasonable fuel, without committing waste.

front: What is a reversion?
back: The future interest left in a grantor who conveys a lesser estate without providing who takes next; always vested, transferable and exempt from the RAP.

front: When is a remainder vested?
back: When it is given to an ascertained person and subject to no condition precedent other than the natural end of the prior estate.

front: Name the three kinds of vested remainder.
back: Indefeasibly vested; vested subject to open (a class that can grow); vested subject to complete divestment (a condition subsequent can take it away).

front: When is a remainder contingent?
back: When the taker is unborn or unascertained, or the remainder is subject to a condition precedent; the grantor then keeps a reversion.

front: What is the 'comma test' for vested vs. contingent remainders?
back: A condition in the same clause as the gift ('to B if B survives A') is a condition precedent (contingent); a condition after a complete gift ('to B, but if B dies before A, to C') is a condition subsequent (vested subject to divestment).

front: Distinguish shifting and springing executory interests.
back: Shifting: divests a prior transferee. Springing: divests the grantor (or follows a gap). Both are transferee interests subject to the RAP.

front: State the Rule in Shelley's Case and its modern status.
back: 'To A for life, then to A's heirs' gave A a fee simple. Abolished in most states; in California the heirs take as remaindermen (Civ. Code § 779).

front: State the Doctrine of Worthier Title and its California status.
back: 'To A for life, then to O's heirs' leaves a reversion in O, not a remainder in O's heirs. California has no worthier-title rule (Prob. Code § 21108).

front: When does a class close under the rule of convenience?
back: When any class member is entitled to demand possession of a share; later-born members are excluded, but those in gestation are included.

front: State the common-law rule against perpetuities.
back: No interest is good unless it must vest, if at all, not later than 21 years after some life in being at the creation of the interest.

front: Which interests are exempt from the RAP?
back: Interests in the grantor (reversion, possibility of reverter, right of entry), indefeasibly vested remainders, vested remainders subject to complete divestment, charity-to-charity gifts, and options in a lease to buy the leased land.

front: Which interests are subject to the RAP?
back: Contingent remainders, executory interests, vested remainders subject to open (class gifts), options in gross and (majority) rights of first refusal.

front: Why does 'to A for life, then to A's children who reach 25' fail at common law when A is alive?
back: A could have a child after the grant who reaches 25 more than 21 years after A and every other life in being die; class gifts are all-or-nothing.

front: What is the fertile octogenarian trap?
back: Everyone is conclusively presumed capable of having children regardless of age, so a gift that depends on no more children being born can fail.

front: What is the unborn widow trap?
back: A gift to a person's 'widow' may describe someone not yet born at the grant, so interests that wait for the widow's death can vest too late.

front: How does California's USRAP change the RAP?
back: An interest is valid if it satisfies the common-law rule or actually vests or terminates within 90 years after creation; otherwise a court reforms it (Prob. Code §§ 21205, 21220). Most nondonative transfers are excluded (§ 21225).

front: Which restraints on alienation of a fee are void?
back: Disabling restraints are void; forfeiture and promissory restraints on a fee are generally void. Reasonable restraints (ROFRs, lease consent clauses, co-op approvals) are valid.

front: Are contingent remainders and executory interests transferable today?
back: Yes, by deed, will and descent, unless survival is a condition of the interest (Civ. Code § 699 in California).

front: What concurrent estate is presumed when land is conveyed to two people?
back: Tenancy in common: separate undivided shares, no survivorship, unity of possession only.

front: What are the four unities of a joint tenancy?
back: Time, title, interest and possession, plus clear language creating a right of survivorship.

front: What does California require to create a joint tenancy?
back: It must be expressly declared in the transfer; an owner may create one by conveying to herself and another (Civ. Code § 683).

front: A, B and C are joint tenants. A deeds to D. Then B dies with a will leaving all to E. Who owns what?
back: D owns one-third as a tenant in common. B's will is ineffective; C takes B's share by survivorship and holds two-thirds as a tenant in common with D.

front: Can a joint tenant sever by deeding to herself in California?
back: Yes (Riddle v. Harmon). To defeat survivorship, the instrument must be recorded before death, or executed within 3 days before death and recorded within 7 days after (Civ. Code § 683.2).

front: Does one joint tenant's mortgage sever the joint tenancy?
back: Title theory: yes. Lien theory (majority and California): no; if the mortgagor dies first, the survivor takes free of the lien (People v. Nogarr).

front: Does a lease by one joint tenant sever in California?
back: No; the lease ends when the lessor-joint tenant dies (Tenhet v. Boswell).

front: Does California recognize tenancy by the entirety?
back: No. Spouses hold community property (with or without right of survivorship), joint tenancy or tenancy in common.

front: Does a cotenant in sole possession owe rent to the others?
back: No, absent ouster or agreement (majority). Rents collected from third parties and profits from extracting resources must be shared.

front: What is ouster?
back: A cotenant's refusal to admit another cotenant who demands possession, or an express claim of exclusive ownership communicated to the others; it triggers rent liability and starts adverse possession.

front: Can a cotenant compel contribution for taxes, mortgage, repairs and improvements?
back: Taxes and mortgage payments: yes, offset by the value of exclusive occupancy. Repairs and improvements: no affirmative right; credit only in partition or accounting (improvements: value added).

front: What does California's Partition of Real Property Act add?
back: For tenancies in common without a governing agreement, in actions filed on or after Jan 1, 2023: cotenant buyout at appraised value, preference for partition in kind, and open-market sale through a broker (CCP § 874.311 et seq.).

front: Name the four leasehold estates.
back: Tenancy for years (fixed end), periodic tenancy (until notice), tenancy at will (either may end), tenancy at sufferance (holdover).

front: How much notice ends a periodic tenancy at common law and in California?
back: Common law: one full period (six months for year to year), ending at a period's end. California: at least the period, max 30 days; residential landlord gives 60 days if the tenant has occupied a year or more (Civ. Code §§ 1946, 1946.1).

front: What may a landlord do when a tenant holds over?
back: Evict (with damages for the holdover period) or bind the tenant to a new periodic tenancy on the same terms (majority: year to year if the original term was a year or more).

front: Contrast the English and American rules on delivery of possession.
back: English (majority): landlord must deliver actual possession; tenant may terminate or affirm with abatement and damages. American: landlord need deliver only the legal right; tenant sues the holdover.

front: What is California's residential security-deposit cap after July 1, 2024?
back: One month's rent (two months for small landlords who are natural persons or LLCs of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units; one month for service members); return within 21 days (Civ. Code § 1950.5).

front: What are the tenant's basic duties?
back: Pay rent, avoid waste, make ordinary repairs (absent contrary lease or statute), and not use the premises illegally.

front: What may a landlord do when a tenant abandons?
back: Accept surrender and end the lease; relet for the tenant's account and sue for the deficiency; or (traditional) leave it vacant and sue for rent. The modern majority requires reasonable mitigation.

front: Who bears the burden on mitigation in California?
back: The tenant must prove the amount of rent that could reasonably have been avoided (Civ. Code § 1951.2); a lock-in remedy is available only if the lease provides it and allows reasonable transfers (§ 1951.4).

front: What is the effect of a partial actual eviction by the landlord?
back: At common law the tenant's entire rent obligation is suspended while the eviction continues, even though the tenant stays in the rest of the premises.

front: State the elements of constructive eviction.
back: Landlord's act or breach of duty that substantially interferes with use and enjoyment; notice and failure to cure; tenant vacates within a reasonable time.

front: What does the implied warranty of habitability require, and can it be waived?
back: Residential premises fit for human habitation (housing-code and health and safety standards) at the start and throughout the lease; it cannot be waived (Green v. Superior Court; Civ. Code §§ 1941, 1942.1).

front: List the tenant's remedies for breach of habitability.
back: Terminate; repair and deduct; withhold or reduce rent; damages (reduced rental value); defense to eviction for nonpayment.

front: What are California's repair-and-deduct limits?
back: After notice and a reasonable time (30 days presumed), up to one month's rent, no more than twice in any 12-month period (Civ. Code § 1942).

front: What is California's retaliatory eviction presumption?
back: Retaliation is presumed if the landlord acts within 180 days after the tenant's protected activity, unless the tenant is in rent default (Civ. Code § 1942.5).

front: Distinguish assignment from sublease.
back: Assignment transfers the entire remaining term; sublease transfers less, so the tenant keeps a reversion (majority objective test).

front: After an assignment, who is liable to the landlord for rent?
back: Original tenant: privity of contract (surety) for the whole term. Assignee: privity of estate while it holds the leasehold (until reassignment); if it assumed, privity of contract for the whole term. Sublessee: not liable directly.

front: When does a lease covenant run to assignees?
back: When the parties intended it to run, it touches and concerns the land, and there is privity of estate (Spencer's Case).

front: Does a tenant's covenant to insure run with the leasehold?
back: Usually yes when the proceeds are to restore or benefit the premises; a bare promise to pay money unconnected to the land may be personal.

front: May a landlord arbitrarily refuse consent to assignment?
back: Traditional rule: yes. Modern trend and California: not where the lease requires consent without a standard (Kendall v. Ernest Pestana; Civ. Code § 1995.260), unless the lease expressly prohibits transfer or sets its own standard.

front: What is the rule in Dumpor's Case?
back: Once a landlord consents to one assignment, the restriction is waived for later assignments unless reserved; many states reject it.

front: What happens to a lease when the landlord sells the building?
back: The buyer takes subject to the lease, gets the rent and the benefit of running tenant covenants, and is bound by the landlord's covenants that touch and concern the land.

front: May a California landlord change the locks on a defaulting tenant?
back: No. Self-help is prohibited; the landlord must use unlawful detainer and faces statutory damages for lockouts and utility shutoffs (Civ. Code § 789.3).

front: List the common-law exceptions to landlord tort immunity.
back: Concealed latent defects known to the landlord; common areas; negligent repairs; premises leased for public use; short-term furnished dwellings; (modern) landlord's covenant to repair.

front: What duty does a California landlord owe for conditions on the premises?
back: Ordinary negligence (Rowland); no strict liability for latent defects (Peterson v. Superior Court); dog cases need actual knowledge and power to remove (Uccello).

front: What does California's Tenant Protection Act require?
back: For covered residential units after 12 months of occupancy: just cause to terminate (with relocation help for no-fault causes), and rent increases capped at the lesser of 5% + CPI or 10%; scheduled to sunset Jan 1, 2030 (Civ. Code §§ 1946.2, 1947.12).

front: What is surrender by operation of law?
back: The landlord's conduct inconsistent with the continuing lease (e.g., retaking the premises for its own use) accepts the tenant's offer to surrender and ends future rent liability.

front: What are the Fair Housing Act's two main owner exemptions?
back: A single-family house sold or rented by an owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or discriminatory ads; and an owner-occupied dwelling of four or fewer units. The advertising ban (§ 3604(c)) still applies.

front: Which law governs title to land in a multistate dispute?
back: The law of the situs governs conveyances, estates, recording, liens, adverse possession and succession to land; a court with personal jurisdiction may order a party to convey land elsewhere.

front: List the requirements for the burden of a real covenant to run.
back: Writing, intent, touch and concern, horizontal privity, vertical privity, and notice.

front: What is horizontal privity?
back: A relationship between the original covenanting parties created by a conveyance of an interest in land (grantor-grantee or landlord-tenant); neighbors' bare agreements lack it.

front: What is needed for the benefit of a real covenant to run?
back: Writing, intent, touch and concern and (relaxed) vertical privity; horizontal privity is not required.

front: List the requirements for an equitable servitude to bind a successor.
back: Writing (or common scheme), intent, touch and concern, and notice; no privity. Remedy: injunction.

front: When does a common scheme bind a lot whose deed lacks the restriction?
back: Majority: when a general plan existed when sales began and the buyer had actual, record or inquiry notice (Sanborn v. McLean).

front: What is California's rule on implied reciprocal servitudes?
back: No servitude is implied from a plan alone; it must be in a recorded instrument (Riley v. Bear Creek). Recorded CC&Rs bind later buyers even if their deeds are silent (Citizens for Covenant Compliance).

front: Do HOA assessment covenants touch and concern the land?
back: Yes, when the money maintains or improves the land or common areas (Neponsit).

front: Does a home business violate a 'residential purposes only' covenant?
back: Usually if it brings customers, employees, signs or traffic that change the residential character; incidental home-office work usually does not.

front: List the defenses to enforcement of a covenant or servitude.
back: Changed conditions, abandonment, acquiescence, laches, unclean hands, estoppel, release, merger, prescription, condemnation, expiration.

front: When do changed conditions terminate a restriction?
back: Only when the change is so radical that the restriction can no longer achieve its purpose, judged mainly within the restricted area; a drop in value or outside change is not enough.

front: What standard applies to a recorded restriction in a California CID?
back: Presumed reasonable; enforced unless arbitrary, unduly burdensome relative to benefits, or against fundamental public policy, judged for the whole development (Nahrstedt).

front: Distinguish a condominium from a cooperative.
back: Condo: fee in the unit plus a tenancy in common in common areas. Co-op: corporation owns the building; residents hold shares and proprietary leases; board approval of transfers generally valid.

front: Distinguish an easement appurtenant from one in gross.
back: Appurtenant benefits a dominant parcel and passes with it; in gross benefits its holder personally or commercially. Courts prefer appurtenant.

front: What is a license, and when is it irrevocable?
back: Revocable permission to enter, not an interest in land. Irrevocable if coupled with an interest or if the licensee substantially and foreseeably relied (easement by estoppel).

front: Can an easement be reserved in favor of a third party?
back: Common law: no. Modern trend and California: yes, if intended (Willard v. First Church of Christ, Scientist).

front: State the elements of an easement implied from prior use.
back: Common ownership then severance; prior use that was apparent and continuous at severance; reasonable necessity (strict for reservations in many states).

front: State the elements of an easement by necessity.
back: Common ownership, severance, and strict necessity (e.g., landlocked) at severance; it ends when the necessity ends.

front: State the elements of a prescriptive easement.
back: Use that is open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, and adverse (without permission) for the statutory period; exclusivity not required.

front: How long is the prescriptive period in California, and must taxes be paid?
back: Five years; no tax payment unless the easement was separately assessed (Civ. Code § 1007; Gilardi v. Hallam).

front: How can a California owner prevent prescriptive easements?
back: Post signs stating 'Right to pass by permission, and subject to control, of owner' at entrances or every 200 feet (Civ. Code § 1008), or record a notice of consent (§ 813).

front: Can an easement holder subdivide the dominant estate and add utilities?
back: Increased use from normal development is a change in degree and usually allowed; a new kind of use (utility lines over an access easement) is usually outside scope.

front: May an easement be used to benefit land other than the dominant estate?
back: No (Brown v. Voss); the remedy is injunction or damages, not termination.

front: Does an appurtenant easement pass if the deed does not mention it?
back: Yes, automatically with the dominant estate; the burden binds servient successors with notice.

front: How is an easement terminated by abandonment?
back: Nonuse plus conduct showing intent to abandon; nonuse alone is not enough for an express easement. California: nonuse for five years extinguishes a prescriptive easement (Civ. Code § 811).

front: List the ways an easement ends.
back: Terms, merger, release, abandonment, estoppel, prescription, end of necessity, condemnation, destruction of a servient structure, BFP without notice.

front: What test decides whether a chattel is a fixture?
back: Objective intent shown by degree of annexation, adaptation to the land's use, and damage on removal.

front: May a tenant remove trade fixtures?
back: Yes, before the lease ends, if removal does not substantially damage the premises, repairing any damage (Civ. Code § 1019).

front: When does a fixture-filing security interest beat an earlier mortgage?
back: A purchase-money security interest perfected by fixture filing before the goods become fixtures or within 20 days after has priority over earlier real-property interests, except a construction mortgage (UCC § 9-334).

front: What test does a zoning ordinance have to pass?
back: Rational relation to a legitimate public purpose (Euclid), within enabling authority and consistent with the general plan, without violating constitutional rights or the FHA.

front: What are the limits on a nonconforming use?
back: It may continue but not substantially expand or change; it ends by abandonment or substantial destruction; many states (including California) allow a reasonable amortization period.

front: When may a variance be granted?
back: When strict application causes unnecessary hardship from conditions unique to the property, not self-created, without harm to the neighborhood. California bars use variances (Gov. Code § 65906).

front: What is spot zoning?
back: Rezoning a small parcel for a use inconsistent with the comprehensive plan, for private benefit; invalid.

front: What must a writing contain to satisfy the statute of frauds for a land sale?
back: Signed by the party to be charged; identifies the parties, describes the land and states the price.

front: What acts satisfy the part-performance exception?
back: Acts unequivocally referable to the contract, usually two of possession, payment and substantial improvements.

front: Is time of the essence in a land contract?
back: Not unless the contract says so, circumstances show it, or a party makes it so by notice; a party may close within a reasonable time and pay delay damages.

front: What makes title unmarketable?
back: Reasonable doubt exposing the buyer to litigation: chain-of-title gaps, unadjudicated adverse possession title, encumbrances (mortgages, easements, covenants), significant encroachments, existing zoning violations. Zoning restrictions alone do not.

front: When must the seller's title be marketable?
back: At closing; the seller may cure before then (e.g., paying off a mortgage with sale proceeds). Under an installment contract, at the final payment.

front: What is California's 3% liquidated damages rule?
back: In a residential purchase of 1–4 units the buyer intends to occupy, a deposit of up to 3% of the price in a separately initialed clause is presumed valid (Civ. Code §§ 1675, 1677).

front: Who bears risk of loss between contract and closing?
back: Majority: buyer (equitable conversion), with credit for seller's insurance. California (UVPRA, Civ. Code § 1662): seller, until legal title or possession passes.

front: How must an option be exercised?
back: Strictly according to its terms and within its time; an option in a lease runs with the leasehold.

front: What is a right of first refusal?
back: A right to buy on the same terms as a bona fide third-party offer the owner wishes to accept; a buyer with notice takes subject to it.

front: What must a seller of a used home disclose?
back: Majority: known material latent defects not reasonably discoverable by the buyer; liable for misrepresentation and active concealment despite a general 'as is' clause.

front: What is the doctrine of merger?
back: On acceptance of the deed, title promises in the contract merge into the deed; collateral promises, fraud and express survival clauses survive.

front: What is the lien theory of mortgages?
back: The mortgagee holds only a lien; the mortgagor keeps title and possession until foreclosure (majority; California, Civ. Code § 2927).

front: When is an absolute deed treated as a mortgage?
back: When it was given as security for a debt, shown by parol evidence (clear and convincing): prior debt, low price, grantor stays in possession, repurchase right. The grantee must foreclose.

front: How do modern courts limit forfeiture under installment land contracts?
back: Grace or cure periods, restitution of excess payments, waiver by accepting late payments, or treatment as a mortgage. California: buyer who paid a substantial part may redeem by paying the balance (Petersen v. Hartell).

front: Why does a purchase-money mortgage beat a prior judgment lien against the buyer?
back: The judgment lien attaches only when the buyer acquires title, and the purchase-money mortgage given as part of the acquisition takes priority (Civ. Code § 2898), subject to the recording laws.

front: Do future advances under a recorded mortgage keep their priority?
back: Obligatory advances do; optional advances made with actual notice of an intervening lien are subordinate to it (majority).

front: What is clogging the equity of redemption?
back: A term in the original mortgage that cuts off or restricts the mortgagor's right to redeem before sale (e.g., lender's option to buy); void.

front: Distinguish 'subject to' from 'assumption' when mortgaged land is sold.
back: 'Subject to': no personal liability for the buyer; the land remains liable. 'Assumes': buyer personally liable to the lender as principal; original mortgagor remains a surety.

front: Are due-on-sale clauses enforceable?
back: Yes under the Garn–St Germain Act (12 U.S.C. § 1701j-3), subject to residential exceptions (spouse/children, death, divorce, inter vivos trust, junior liens, short leases).

front: Does an assignment of the mortgage without the note transfer anything?
back: Majority: no; the mortgage follows the note, and transfer of the note carries the mortgage.

front: What is the main risk of a deed in lieu of foreclosure for the lender?
back: It takes title subject to junior liens, which only foreclosure would extinguish.

front: What does foreclosure do to senior and junior interests?
back: Extinguishes the foreclosed mortgage and junior interests joined or noticed; senior interests are unaffected and the buyer takes subject to them; omitted juniors survive.

front: In what order are foreclosure proceeds distributed?
back: Costs of sale, the foreclosing debt, junior interests in order of priority, then any surplus to the mortgagor.

front: Distinguish equitable and statutory redemption.
back: Equitable: before sale, pay the full (accelerated) debt; cannot be clogged. Statutory: after sale, for a set period, pay the sale price.

front: What are California's main anti-deficiency rules?
back: One-action rule (CCP § 726); no deficiency after a trustee's sale (§ 580d); none on purchase-money loans (§ 580b); fair-value limit after judicial sale; not waivable in advance.

front: What is the redemption period after a California judicial foreclosure sale?
back: One year if the proceeds do not satisfy the debt (deficiency possible); three months if they do; none after a trustee's sale (CCP § 729.030).

front: State the elements of adverse possession.
back: Actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile, and continuous possession for the statutory period.

front: What extra requirements does California impose for adverse possession?
back: Five years plus timely payment of all taxes levied and assessed during the period; color of title, or occupation by substantial enclosure or usual cultivation or improvement (CCP §§ 318, 322–325).

front: When may adverse possessors tack their periods?
back: When they are in privity: possession passed by deed, will, inheritance or voluntary transfer, not by abandonment or ouster.

front: Do disabilities stop the adverse-possession clock?
back: Only disabilities existing when possession began (minority, insanity, imprisonment); later disabilities do not.

front: What is the agreed-boundary doctrine, and how does California apply it?
back: Uncertainty, agreement fixing a line, and acceptance bind neighbors to the line. California applies it narrowly, not where records fix the true line (Bryant v. Blevins).

front: What must a valid deed contain?
back: Writing, grantor's signature, identified grantor and grantee, adequate description, words of present grant, and delivery; consideration and witnesses unnecessary.

front: In what order do description elements control?
back: Natural monuments, artificial monuments, courses, distances, then area.

front: What is delivery of a deed?
back: Words or conduct showing the grantor's intent that the deed be presently operative; physical transfer and recording raise a presumption of delivery.

front: What happens when a deed is handed to the grantee subject to an oral condition?
back: Majority: the condition is ineffective and the delivery is absolute (California Civ. Code § 1056).

front: Name the six covenants of a general warranty deed and when each is breached.
back: Present (at delivery): seisin, right to convey, against encumbrances. Future (on eviction): warranty, quiet enjoyment, further assurances.

front: What covenants does a California grant deed imply?
back: That the grantor has not previously conveyed the same estate, and that it is free from encumbrances done, made or suffered by the grantor or those claiming under the grantor (Civ. Code § 1113).

front: What is estoppel by deed?
back: A grantor who conveys land she does not own and later acquires it is estopped to deny the grant; title passes to the grantee (Civ. Code § 1106). Not for quitclaims.

front: Which deeds are void even against a BFP?
back: Forged deeds, undelivered (stolen) deeds, deeds by adjudicated incompetents, and fraud in the factum.

front: Compare race, notice and race-notice statutes.
back: Race: first to record wins. Notice: later BFP without notice wins. Race-notice: later BFP without notice wins only if it records first.

front: What type of recording act does California have?
back: Race-notice (Civ. Code § 1214); leases of one year or less are excluded.

front: Who is a bona fide purchaser?
back: A purchaser or mortgagee for value (not a donee, heir or devisee) who takes without actual, record or inquiry notice of the earlier interest when paying value.

front: What facts give inquiry notice?
back: Possession by someone other than the seller, references in recorded instruments to unrecorded interests, and visible physical evidence such as a path or pipe.

front: What is a wild deed?
back: A recorded deed from someone whose own acquisition was never recorded; it is outside the chain of title and gives no constructive notice.

front: What is the shelter rule?
back: One who takes from a BFP is protected even with notice, except a prior wrongdoer who reacquires.

front: Does title insurance run with the land to a later buyer?
back: No; the owner's policy protects only the named insured (and limited successors such as heirs); the lender's policy follows the loan.

front: When does a judgment lien attach to the debtor's land?
back: On recording or docketing in the county, to land owned then or later acquired, but only to the debtor's actual interest; California abstract liens last ten years (CCP § 697.310).
